sections.heading: Learning to bring everything to you
sections.text:
God, you hear me when I come to you. Teach me to live not only by accepting what you provide and allow, but by actually bringing my life to you in prayer—my soul, my body, my children, my family, and my church.

Make my heart willing to be shaped by what you want. Let prayer become the way I live before you, so that I honor you and am guarded from evil, including the evil I do not even recognize in myself.
theological_themes: God welcomes prayer; prayer belongs in every part of ordinary life; God’s providence and prayer are not enemies but belong together; the heart needs to be shaped by God’s will; God protects his people from seen and unseen evil.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells believers to bring every concern to God with prayer and thanksgiving, and he connects that prayer with God’s guarding peace. This supports the prayer’s desire to bring all of life before God rather than live self-sufficiently.

Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for God’s name, kingdom, will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil. That pattern grounds the prayer’s movement from daily dependence to surrender and protection.

sections.heading: Seeing my sin without losing sight of your good purposes
sections.text:
Help me see honestly that sin clings even to the good things I do. Keep me from pretending my motives are cleaner than they are.

At the same time, teach me to receive something good from everything you put in my path. Even when circumstances expose what is wrong in me, use them to draw me nearer to you and make me wiser in your ways.
theological_themes: The believer remains dependent on grace because sin still affects motives and actions; God can use all circumstances, including humbling ones, for spiritual good; self-knowledge should lead to dependence rather than despair.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the painful reality that sin remains present even when he desires to do good, and he turns from self-reliance to deliverance through Christ. This supports the prayer’s honest confession that sin accompanies even good actions.
Paul teaches that God works all things for the good of those who love him, with that good defined by conformity to Christ. This grounds the request to gain spiritual good from whatever God allows.

sections.heading: Letting prayer change my will, not trying to manage yours
sections.text:
Teach me that prayer is not my way of bending you to my plans. Its work is to bring my will into line with yours.

When I pray as if you must agree with me, I am acting as though I know better than Christ. That is pride, and I confess it as sin. Save me from using prayer to stay in control while pretending to trust you.
theological_themes: Prayer is an act of submission, not control; Christ is Lord and wiser than the believer; pride can corrupt even religious activity; true prayer seeks God’s will above personal preference.

scripture_references.connection: In Gethsemane, Jesus brings his real desire to the Father while submitting himself to the Father’s will. His prayer gives the pattern for honest petition joined to surrender.
James warns that prayer can be disordered by selfish desires. This directly supports the confession that prayer becomes sinful when it is used to serve my own agenda rather than God’s will.

sections.heading: Praying by what you command and promise
sections.text:
Keep me praying according to what you have told me to ask for and what you have promised to give. I do not need to force your hand. I need to trust your word and leave myself in your hands.

When you command me to ask for forgiveness, peace, and a broken and teachable heart, you are not mocking me. You call me to ask because you are willing to give what brings glory to you and real good to me.
theological_themes: Prayer rests on God’s commands and promises; God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; forgiveness, peace, and repentance are gifts God delights to give; God’s glory and the believer’s good belong together.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches confidence in prayer when believers ask according to God’s will. This grounds the prayer’s emphasis on praying by God’s revealed will rather than by presumption.
John connects confession with God’s faithful forgiveness and cleansing. This supports the confidence that when God calls me to seek pardon, he is ready to give it in Christ.
God promises to give his people a new heart and Spirit-led obedience. This illuminates the request for brokenness and a heart made responsive to God.

sections.heading: Asking boldly for more than small comforts
sections.text:
Do not let my prayers shrink down to only small personal comforts. Give me holy boldness to ask for great things—for your people and for me—not so that we can look impressive, but so that our lives would make your glory visible.

Make me willing to want what would honor you most, even when it stretches my faith and exposes how small my desires have become.
theological_themes: Believers are invited to pray boldly; prayer should seek the good of God’s people as well as personal needs; the ultimate aim of answered prayer is God’s glory; faith expands desire beyond private comfort.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God as able to do far more than believers ask or imagine, and he connects that abundance to God’s glory in the church and in Christ. This supports asking boldly for great things for God’s people.
Jesus links abiding in him with effective prayer, fruitfulness, and the Father’s glory. This grounds the desire that answered prayer would produce lives that display God’s glory.

sections.heading: Coming freely, remembering your ways, and refusing my own cravings
sections.text:
Teach me that it is wise to pray about everything I have and everything I need—not because I am forced to, but because I love you and belong to you. Let me come to you at any time and lay my needs open before you without fear.

My great sin is how easily I lose the taste and weight of your ways. Bring that truth back to my mind, because remembering it helps me live aware of your nearness.

And Father, do not hand me over to myself. There is no misery like being ruled by my own desires for my own ends. Govern me by your Spirit instead, and teach me to want what leads to life.
theological_themes: Prayer is free access to the Father through grace; love, not mere necessity, should draw the believer to God; forgetting the beauty of God’s ways dulls awareness of his presence; being ruled by sinful desires is a severe form of judgment; the Spirit’s rule leads to life.

scripture_references.connection: Because of Christ our high priest, believers are invited to approach God’s throne with confidence for mercy and help. This supports coming freely and honestly with needs at any time.

Jesus connects love for him, keeping his commandments, and the experience of his self-disclosure to the believer. This supports the idea that treasuring and remembering God’s ways is tied to a living sense of his presence.

Paul describes God’s judgment as giving people over to the desires they have chosen in exchange for God. This grounds the prayer’s severe warning that being ruled by one’s own lusts is itself a terrible form of wrath.

Paul contrasts living by the flesh with putting sin to death by the Spirit, and identifies those led by the Spirit as God’s children. This supports the final request to be governed by the Spirit rather than by sinful desires.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly holds together divine providence, sovereign will, and real prayer. Some Christian traditions nuance this relationship differently, so the adaptation keeps the original’s emphasis without implying that prayer is mechanical or that human choices are meaningless.

The line about God commanding prayer because he will give the promised thing could be misread as a guarantee of every desired outcome. The adaptation frames this around what God has actually commanded and promised—such as forgiveness, peace, repentance, and a changed heart—rather than unrestricted claims.

The phrase about ‘no wrath like the wrath of being governed by my own lusts’ is severe. The adaptation preserves its force by connecting it to the biblical theme of God handing people over to their desires, while avoiding language that would make every experience of temptation itself equal to divine wrath.
significant_interpretive_choices: ‘God of the open ear’ was rendered as God who hears when I come to him, preserving the confidence of access without retaining the archaic phrase.

‘Live by prayer as well as by providence’ was interpreted as refusing to set prayer against God’s ordering of circumstances; the modern prayer asks to receive providence while actively bringing all of life to God.
‘The good I can distil from everything’ was interpreted not as finding pleasant outcomes in everything, but as God using all circumstances to produce spiritual good and conformity to Christ.

‘Savour of thy ways’ was rendered as keeping the taste, weight, and beauty of God’s ways, because the original suggests more than mere intellectual memory; it implies affectionate spiritual perception.
